name: Adaptive Practice With Regrouping
title: Adaptive Practice With Regrouping
answer: Adaptive practice with regrouping is the use of AI math programs that adjust each problem to a student's last answer, paired with a teacher who uses the program's reports to form next-day small groups. It matters because the learning gains from adaptive software are real but modest, and the larger opportunity is in how teachers turn the data into instruction. The software supplies the data, while the teacher supplies the teaching.

sections.body: Adaptive practice is the most common form of AI in math classrooms. Programs change the next problem based on whether a student answered the previous one correctly. The problem it solves is that a single class can contain students who are shaky on a topic and students who are ready to move on. Regrouping solves the follow-through problem by having the teacher use the software's picture of each student to create small groups for the next day. In this model the software does not replace the teacher, it gives the teacher a current map of who needs what.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In elementary grades, the text names Zearn as an example of an adaptive program, and for older students it names Khan Academy. The programs adjust each problem according to the student's last answer. The regrouping step happens when the teacher reads the reports and forms small groups for the next day. For example, a teacher might pull five students for a short lesson on equivalent fractions while the rest of the class continues practicing. The text does not give separate grade-band routines beyond the elementary and older-student examples, but the pattern is the same: software data first, then teacher-led small-group instruction.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book reports a review of 21 studies of AI in kindergarten through 12th grade math that found a small positive effect overall, with larger effects when the software acted as a tutor or adaptive system (Yi et al., 2024). It also reports another review finding that intelligent tutoring helped students in general, but that the advantage shrank when it was compared with other practice software rather than with no software at all (Letourneau, 2025). A mapping of adaptive learning research found that relatively few systems had been put to work on real student problems in real schools (Kabudi et al., 2021). The book's own framing is that the gains are real but modest, which is what a district should expect. It adds that a district switching from one practice program to another should not expect a large jump.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits start with the size of the effect. The text says gains are real but modest, and that switching from one practice program to another should not be expected to produce a large jump. The bigger gains usually come from how teachers use what the software reports, so the instructional decisions stay with the teacher. The software provides the data, and the teacher provides the instruction, including which students to regroup and what to teach them. The text also warns that relatively few adaptive systems have been tested on real student problems in real schools, so schools should ask vendors for evidence from classrooms like their own. A tool that works in a research study may work differently in a crowded sixth grade class with patchy internet, and the pilot method in Chapter 4 is the way to find out.
